question: How did my focus plan change from June to July, and what did I decide to measure next?

route.query: focus plan changes June July measurements

retrieval.warning: Exact quotations prove provenance, not semantic support.

answer: In June, the user attempted a phone-drawer plan for 25-minute work blocks, noting fewer phone checks but not measuring work output; by July 4, a correction superseded that explanation, and on July 18 a new experiment was launched to log minutes from sitting down to starting a concrete action, comparing logs informally. The user decided to measure the time between sitting down and beginning the next action as the next focus metric. [E3] [E4] [E2]

claims.text: In June, the user attempted a phone-drawer plan for 25-minute work blocks, noting fewer phone checks but not measuring work output.
By July 4, a correction superseded the June phone-only explanation.
On July 18, a new experiment was launched to log minutes from sitting down to starting a concrete action, comparing logs informally.
The user decided to measure the time between sitting down and beginning the next action as the next focus metric.

limitations: The June note records an attempt and early interpretation, not evidence that the phone was the main cause of lost time.
The July 18 plan states it is a decision and measurement plan, not a completed experiment; no results are recorded.
The correction on July 4 supersedes the June plan but does not itself provide measured outcomes for the July experiment.

claims.text: In June, the user attempted a phone-drawer plan for 25-minute work blocks, noting fewer phone checks but not measuring work output.

evidence.quote:
# Focus plan, June 10

I thought putting my phone in a drawer would solve most of my study interruptions. My initial plan was to do a 25-minute work block with the phone out of reach, then take a five-minute break. I tried this for three morning sessions. I wrote down fewer phone checks in those sessions, but I did not measure total work completed or compare the sessions with a similar week. This note records an attempt and an early interpretation, not evidence that the phone was the main cause of lost time.

The biggest unresolved question was what happened when I sat down without a clear next action. I sometimes spent the first ten minutes deciding which problem to start. I planned to test that separately. A later note, `life-focus-correction-2026-07-04`, revises my explanation; the drawer plan remains here as history.
evidence.title: 2026-06-10-focus-plan

claims.text: By July 4, a correction superseded the June phone-only explanation.
On July 18, a new experiment was launched to log minutes from sitting down to starting a concrete action, comparing logs informally.

evidence.quote:
# Next focus experiment, July 18

For the next two weeks, I will write the first concrete action on a card before each morning work block, silence notifications for 30 minutes, and log the minutes from sitting down to starting that action. I will compare those logs with my previous sessions, while treating the comparison as informal because task difficulty and location may differ.

This is a decision and a measurement plan, not a completed experiment. I have not recorded the two-week results here. If the logs show little change or the routine is too annoying to keep, I will stop recommending it as my default. This decision draws on the July 4 correction, which superseded my June phone-only explanation.
evidence.title: 2026-07-18-focus-decision
